units.spine: Nothing presses on Rundgate at present, and that owes nothing to luck. The town is kept ready enough that testing it would cost more than it could return.
Everyone in the town knows there is something out past the walls, and nobody speaks of it beyond that. The town takes the quiet itself as proof the arrangement holds.
faces: A drover says nobody here has asked him what he saw on the road, though he always has an answer ready.
The men who hold the ways in bar the gate at dusk without fail, and no one argues the hour with them.
A priest of one of the parishes prays for the men who watch the border in the same breath as the roads.
A clerk in the hall says nothing about the nights beyond the wall has ever reached the hall as a complaint.
The watch says whatever is brought to it at the gate stops there, and goes no further up to the hall.
At the tavern the talk turns on who stands the nights, and the country beyond the wall never comes into it.
A soldier of the garrison says no one from the town ever comes out to watch the drills.
A guild factor reckons the trades pay for the watch kept at the gate, and counts that line as belonging to everyone.
At the market they say the stalls go up the same whatever the country beyond is doing.
A clerk of the court says a dispute over the toll is settled the day it is brought, and the country beyond has never brought one.
The elders say the young stand the nights, and the old are the ones who say how it should be done.

units.poolKey: Invasion & War: walls AND professional garrison
units.spine: A traveller is stopped at the gate and counted before he is let through, and what waits past it is a town that pays soldiers of its own to keep it.
faces: The men who hold the ways in say a stranger pays at the gate, and what is taken there is settled with the hall in its own time.
A clerk in the hall says a stranger who pays at the gate has paid the town in full, whatever he is told at the gate itself.
A clerk of the court holds that anyone who paid the toll may argue it before the court, a stranger the same as a carter.
A traveller says his pack was opened at the gate, and nothing came out of it but the toll.
At the tavern they say the town was never asked whether it wanted soldiers, only what keeping them costs.

units.spine: A court is kept in Rundgate, and no room to hold anyone in it. What the law can take from a man here is his money or his place in the town.
faces: The watch says whatever it finds after dark is settled after dark, there being nowhere to leave a man until morning.
A clerk of the court says the court hears by daylight what the watch already settled in the dark, and nobody asks the court first.
A clerk in the hall reckons the purse has never run to a room to hold a man, and does not say who has asked for one.
A stallholder at the market says a short weight goes before a magistrate and comes back as a sum, and the scales it was weighed on never leave his stall.
A priest of one of the parishes holds that the parish keeps a place for a man once he is dead, and the town keeps none for him while he lives.
A guild factor says a fine is paid out of a man's takings and then forgotten, though the mark it leaves on his standing is not.
At the tavern they say a man with a house here pays his fine and stays, while a man without one goes, and the table loses him.
A traveller says there is nothing here to take from a man who owns nothing in the town. The town has only the one course left open with him.
The men who hold the ways in say they are handed a man and a direction, and given no reason for either.
A soldier of the garrison says what comes against the town is the garrison's business, and the people walked out of it are none of the garrison's concern.

units.spine: Everyone in the town has seen the grain store kept full, and takes it that a crisis would find the place ready.
faces: A clerk in the hall says the hall asks the trades for no more than the trades can carry.
The guilds of the town say the carrying is theirs, and the asking of it is not.
The guilds' reading is the likelier of the two, since the hall has a purse of its own to defend and the guilds only a bill to carry.
The watch holds that the rounds are kept by people still owed for keeping them.
The men who hold the ways in say a cart bound for the grain store is never kept waiting, whatever else is.
A traveller who sits at the tavern hears the grain store praised and the wage complained of, from the same mouths.
At the tavern they say the watch is a trade that drinks on what it is still owed.
A soldier of the garrison holds that a town able to feed itself through a crisis and still short on the garrison's wage has decided something, though it has not said what.
At the market they say a stallholder settles what the hall is owed before settling anything of his own.
A priest of one of the parishes holds that the town keeps its word to the dead before it keeps its word to the living.

units.poolKey: Disasters & Famine: granary AND parish care only
units.spine: A drover says the town looks well provided for from outside. Whoever tends the sick here comes out of the church, there being no house built just for that.
faces: A priest of one of the parishes says a stranger asks for a sick house and is given a person instead, though nobody born here ever asks for the house.
At the market they say grain is hard to keep here for anybody without a door of his own in the town.
At the tavern they say strangers come by just to look at the grain store, and nobody born here ever does.
The watch says strangers often ask where the grain is kept, and nobody has ever asked it where the sick are taken.
A guild factor reckons what a stranger takes for provision is a store the trades filled and have no say in opening.
A clerk of the court says a stranger's questions about the store are ordinary enough, and the ones about the sick are new to the court.

units.spine: A working balance holds in Rundgate. The law is present, crime exists, and neither has the run of the town.

units.poolKey: First-Survey qualification (the reading is a first look)
units.spine: The safety reading for Rundgate is a first one. It is honest about what has been seen and silent about what has not.
A stranger at Rundgate is not robbed outright but is quietly told what the arrangement is, the danger here being organized rather than sudden.
The hall at Rundgate moves against the operators working the town, and the operators move back, with the town caught between the two.
Every way into Rundgate is held at the town's own choosing. What a perimeter buys is not safety outright, but the choice of where anything happens.
A standing force is kept in Rundgate. Their work is the defense of the town, and they are answerable for it as work, not as duty owed.
The town pays for some of its soldiers and knows exactly which ones. They are treated accordingly, paid work rather than sworn duty.
A traveller at Rundgate finds a hall whose business is the kind of trouble a garrison is the wrong tool for, and finds that hall busy.
A traveller at Rundgate is measured at the gate in some way he cannot quite name, and nobody tells him what it was.
The city walls and gates at Rundgate are kept in good repair. What is spent keeping them takes nearly all the town sets aside for defense, and little is left over for anything else.

units.poolKey: Logistics & Supply: Granary with road supply
units.spine: A grain store is kept in Rundgate, and the town is fed by the roads, having no port to draw on instead. The roads are the risk, and the store is what buys time to answer it.
